Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

effort noun

energy put into something, hard work

also make an effort, take pains, it’s worth the effort, worth the effort, a waste of effort, exertion, try one’s best to, I’ll certainly attend to it, I’ll see to it, do one’s best, waste one’s effort, you’ve wasted all your effort, I’ll attend to that, see to it, see to it at once

classical

Cic. Fam. 14.18.2: maximē autem date operam ut valeātis
Plaut. Poen. 332: et oleum et operam perdidī
Traupman 97: make an effort to be on time, dā operam ut tempestīvē adsīs
Traupman 308: it’s (not) worth the effort, pretium operae (nōn) est
Traupman 110: operam dō ut (nē) (+ subjunctive)
Traupman 214: Dā operam eīs rēbus continuō!, see to those things at once!
Traupman 305

opera, operae f.

noun, first declension

effort, pains, work freely given

Operam dare ut, to make an effort to, to see to it that; operam perdere, to waste one’s effort; operae pretium est, it is worth the effort. Lewis & Short: opera “supposes a free will and desire to serve”, where opus is the work itself.

Other words

  • labor, labōris m. — toil, hard work, exertion

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Liv. 21.4.5: nūllō labōre aut corpus fatīgārī aut animus vincī poterat; Cic. de Or. 2.210: magnō illa labōre … esse parta

    Effort as toil, often tiring: magnō labōre, with great effort.

  • ēnītor, ēnītī, ēnīsus sum — make every effort, strive (to)

    verb, third conjugation, deponent; with ut and the subjunctive · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.42: ēnītī et contendere dēbet quam maximē possit, ut vincat; Cic. Fam. 13.29.5; Lael. 59 (Lewis & Short)

    “Make an effort” is often a verb: ēnītī, operam dare, or cōnārī (see try).

  • in magnō negōtiō habēre (+ infinitive) — Traupman’s “take pains to”

    avoid · post-classical · Traupman 109; Suet. Caes. 23 (Lewis & Short s.v. negōtium)

    In Suetonius the phrase means to regard a thing as important, not to take pains over it; for “take pains to” classical Latin says operam dare ut (above).

Examples

  • maximē autem date operam ut valeātis, sī nōs vultis valēre

    above all, make every effort to keep well, if you want us to be wellCic. Fam. 14.18.2

  • sī, quantum operae sūmpsistī ut tuus pistor bonum faceret pānem, ejus duodecimam philosophiae dedissēs, ipse bonus jam prīdem essēs factus

    if you had given philosophy a twelfth of the effort you spent getting your baker to make good bread, you would have become good yourself long agoVarro in Gell. 15.19.2

  • Tum pol ego et oleum et operam perdidī.

    Then, by heaven, I’ve wasted my lamp oil and my effort.Plaut. Poen. 332

  • factūrusne operae pretium sim … nec satis sciō

    whether I shall be doing something worth the effort … I am not quite sureLiv. praef. 1

  • dē geōgraphiā dabō operam ut tibi satisfaciam

    as for the geography, I’ll do my best to satisfy youCic. Att. 2.4.3 (Lewis & Short)

  • Dabō equidem operam.

    I’ll certainly attend to it.Traupman 93

  • Omnem operam perdidistī.

    You’ve wasted all your effort.Traupman 97

  • Eī operam dabō extemplō.

    I’ll attend to that immediately.Traupman 115

  • Operam dō.

    I do my best.Traupman 305

See also try, effort, practice.
